newsitem.title: UK: Intrepid yield hunters target "hyper exotic" debt.
newsitem.headline: Intrepid yield hunters target "hyper exotic" debt.

text.p: In a world where conventional markets offer only paltry yields, investors are braving the fringes of global capital markets.

So-called "basket case" economies from war-torn Liberia to reclusive North Korea are luring adventurous speculators, who are buying unusual and illiquid securities in the hope of huge capital appreciation.

The latest trigger, say traders and analysts, came from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, who made the trade out of traditional markets and into the exotics look too good to resist by providing a stable interest-rate outlook.
"If you needed a green light it was given to you in the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony (to Congress this week)," said David McWilliams, analyst at BNP.

"If you are in the business of borrowing short in dollars and putting it into the exotics, your parameters have been fixed by Mr Greenspan for another few months at least. That play is a bit of a no-brainer."
Much of the debt is defaulted paper carrying a large build-up of deferred interest, with demand driven by expectations of a rescheduling like Poland, Croatia, Mexico and Argentina before them.

The debt of the former Zaire, renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has strengthened substantially in the weeks since President Laurent Kabila took control. It is now trading at some 19 to 21 cents on the dollar, against 11 to 13 cents over a month ago, partly as a result of a buyback at around 11 cents, according to traders.
McWilliams told Reuters prices for hyper-exotic debt had risen on average 10 to 20 percent in recent weeks.
"It is a very ebullient market and it is a wholesale change from what it was a few weeks or months ago."
An exotic debt trader in London said that with developed bond markets range-bound, most fixed income funds are having to go up the credit curve to outperform their benchmarks.

Because the mainstream fund and customer are now more comfortable with risk such as Russia then they were six months or two years ago, spreads have been driven lower, and those looking well into 20 percent yields have to go even further up the credit curve.
"So the real risk hounds are driven out of the room because spreads have come down."

Other countries posting strong gains recently include Sudan, which has seen its paper rise to some 10 cents on the dollar against over seven cents about six weeks ago. Bulgarian Zunk bonds, brought to the market at 40 cents three months ago, are now trading at 70-73.
McWilliams said new funds were coming into the market, at the same time as countries such as Liberia, Sudan and North Korea were coming in from the cold.
"You are getting a fusion of very positive macro factors and it is driving prices through the roof," he said.

McWilliams said demand in the market was being driven partly by American hedge funds. "They have got a gun to their heads. They have to make 20 percent a year, that's their contract, so what you find is that either they sit on the Dow and look for good stocks...or what you get is an increasing amount of them moving into Africa."
The trader said the major players were the trading houses themselves and dedicated punters.

"I would say it is entirely the trading community and a very few select dedicated funds -- people who are refugees from this market over the past decade or 15 years that just can't bring themselves to buy Russian debt at 94 when they saw it trade at 18," he said.
"To that point you are going to get somebody who is tantalised by a low handle of a Liberia, or a Cuba or a North Korea."

McWilliams said a range of countries seemed to be getting their houses in order at the right time. "You have basically got a wall of money building up looking for a home. Into which home they go is predicated on whether or not these countries are getting their act together."
But there is a risk that the market could get ahead of itself, pricing in reform that never materialised.
Supply in the market is patchy, and liquidity remains a problem, but long-term holders of the debt in banks and corporates are coming out of the woodwork as prices rise.

"The guys who have been sitting on it throughout the late eighties and early nineties, who have almost provisioned against it at this stage... Now the Treasurer is saying; 'I can make something here,'" McWilliams said.
